blocks.text: Pretty much every machine learning algorithm speaks one language: numbers. Linear regression multiplies your features by weights and adds them up. K nearest neighbors measures distances between points. A neural network runs matrix multiplication on every input it receives. None of that math works on the string 'red' or the string 'Mumbai'. Before a model can learn from a categorical column like color, city, or plan tier, you have to turn those text labels into numbers it can actually compute with.

This is a genuinely different problem from the category dtype you saw in the changing data types lesson. That lesson was about pandas storing repeated strings more efficiently under the hood, the values were still text as far as any model was concerned. Here, the goal is different: you are producing brand new numeric columns that a model can multiply, add, and measure distances on. Efficient storage and model ready numbers are two separate jobs, and this lesson is entirely about the second one.

blocks.title: Not the same problem as category dtype
blocks.content: astype('category') from the earlier lesson makes a text column cheaper to store in memory. It does not make the column usable by a model that expects numbers. The encoding techniques in this lesson actually replace the text with numeric values a model can compute on.

blocks.alt: Text categories red, blue, and green being converted into the numbers 0, 1, and 2
blocks.caption: Every encoding technique in this lesson exists to solve exactly this conversion problem.

blocks.text: 1. Why Machine Learning Models Need Numbers

Try to picture what a model actually does internally. Linear regression computes a weighted sum of your feature values. Gradient descent nudges those weights by computing a derivative. A distance based algorithm like k nearest neighbors subtracts one row from another and squares the result. Every one of those operations is arithmetic, and arithmetic needs numbers, not the word 'red' or the string 'Mumbai'.

items: A color column: red, blue, green
A city column: Mumbai, Delhi, Pune
A subscription tier: free, basic, premium
An education level: high school, bachelors, masters
A customer satisfaction rating: low, medium, high

blocks.text: Feed a raw text column straight into most scikit-learn models and you will not get a gentle warning, you will get a hard crash.

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(df[["color"]], df["price"])
# ValueError: could not convert string to float: 'red'

blocks.text: That error is the whole reason this lesson exists. Encoding is the step that turns 'red' into something a model can actually multiply. There are two main families of technique for doing this, and picking the wrong one for your data is one of the most common, and most quietly damaging, mistakes in a feature engineering pipeline.

This conversion step is usually called encoding, and it sits right after you have cleaned up data types, the lesson right before this one, and right before you actually train a model. Get the encoding wrong and every downstream step inherits the mistake, no matter how careful the rest of your pipeline is.
2. Label Encoding: Turning Categories Into Integers

Label encoding is the simplest possible idea: look at every unique value in a column, and assign each one a plain integer, 0, 1, 2, and so on. 'red' might become 0, 'blue' might become 1, 'green' might become 2. The column keeps the same number of rows, it just holds integers instead of strings now.

blocks.alt: Label encoding assigning the arbitrary integers 0, 1, and 2 to the categories red, blue, and green
blocks.caption: Each unique category gets one integer. Nothing about the assignment is meaningful yet.

blocks.text: 2.1 Label Encoding With pandas factorize()

pandas' own factorize() function is the fastest way to label encode a column. It returns two things: an array of integer codes, one per row, and an array of the unique labels in the order it assigned them.

code.content:
codes, uniques = pd.factorize(df["color"])
print(codes)     # array([0, 1, 2, 0, 1])
print(uniques)   # Index(['red', 'blue', 'green'], dtype='object')

df["color_encoded"] = codes

blocks.text: factorize() assigns codes in the order each value first appears in the column, not alphabetically and not by any meaningful real world order. That detail matters a lot later in this lesson.

blocks.title: factorize() has a quirk with missing values
blocks.content: Any NaN in the original column gets the code -1 in the output, not a new separate category, and it does not appear in the uniques array either. Keep that in mind if your column still has missing values when you encode it. Handle them deliberately, either before or after, rather than letting a silent -1 slip into your feature.

blocks.text: 2.2 Label Encoding With scikit-learn LabelEncoder

scikit-learn's LabelEncoder does the same basic job, but it fits naturally into an sklearn pipeline and, importantly, lets you fit on your training data and then apply that exact same mapping to your test data with transform().

code.content:
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder

encoder = LabelEncoder()
df["color_encoded"] = encoder.fit_transform(df["color"])

print(encoder.classes_)
# array(['blue', 'green', 'red'], dtype=object), sorted alphabetically

new_codes = encoder.transform(["blue"])  # reuses the exact same mapping

blocks.text: Notice LabelEncoder sorts alphabetically by default, while factorize() goes by order of first appearance. Different rule, same underlying idea, and neither one produces an order that is meaningful by itself.
Both tools do fundamentally the same job, but a few practical differences decide which one fits your workflow better.

blocks.text: 3. The Danger: Label Encoding Implies a False Ordering

Here is the part of label encoding that trips up a lot of people. Once 'red' becomes 0, 'blue' becomes 1, and 'green' becomes 2, a model has no way of knowing those numbers were assigned arbitrarily. All it sees is a numeric column, and to a numeric column, 1 genuinely sits between 0 and 2, and the gap from 0 to 1 is the same size as the gap from 1 to 2.

blocks.alt: A number line showing 0, 1, and 2 with a warning that a model reads blue as sitting between red and green
blocks.caption: The model has no idea this ordering was arbitrary. It just sees numbers, and treats them like numbers.

blocks.text: That is a completely made up relationship. Blue is not literally between red and green. Green is not twice as far from red as blue is. But plenty of algorithms will happily compute exactly that fake relationship and treat it as real. Linear and logistic regression will fit a single coefficient assuming a steady numeric trend across the categories. Distance based algorithms like k nearest neighbors and k means clustering will compute distances where the gap between color codes 0 and 2 is silently treated as twice the gap between 0 and 1. Tree based models like decision trees and random forests are somewhat more forgiving, since they just pick split thresholds rather than computing distances, but even they can end up with strange, hard to interpret splits from an ordering that never should have existed.

code.content:
red, blue, green = 0, 1, 2
print(abs(red - blue))    # 1
print(abs(red - green))   # 2, model reads green as "further" from red than blue is

blocks.title: This is a genuinely common, genuinely costly mistake
blocks.content: Label encoding a non-ordinal column like color, city, or product category and feeding it straight into a distance based or linear model is one of the most frequent silent bugs in real feature engineering work. The model will still train and still produce predictions, it will just be learning from a relationship that was never actually there.

blocks.text: 4. When Label Encoding Is Actually Correct: Ordinal Categories

None of this means label encoding is a bad technique, it means it is the wrong technique for the wrong kind of column. Some categorical columns have a genuine, real world order baked into them. Think of a size column with small, medium, and large, or a satisfaction rating of low, medium, and high, or an education level of high school, bachelors, and masters. In every one of these, the order is not made up, it reflects something true about the data.

blocks.alt: Label encoding correctly matching the real world order of small, medium, and large as 0, 1, and 2
blocks.caption: When the order is genuinely real, label encoding captures it correctly instead of inventing it.

blocks.text: For a column like this, the numeric distance actually means something. Large genuinely is further from small than medium is, in the exact sense the encoding implies. This is the one situation where label encoding is not just acceptable, it is the right tool for the job.

There is one important catch. Both factorize() and LabelEncoder assign codes by order of appearance or alphabetically, not by the meaningful order you actually care about. If you let either one run on a size column without guidance, you might get 'medium' as 0 just because it appeared first in the dataset, which quietly breaks the whole point. For a true ordinal column, you need to specify the order explicitly.
The same explicit mapping approach works for any ordinal column, not just size. A customer satisfaction rating of low, medium, and high follows exactly the same pattern.

blocks.title: Never trust the default order on an ordinal column
blocks.content: factorize() and LabelEncoder both ignore the real world meaning of your categories. For genuinely ordinal data, always build an explicit mapping dictionary yourself instead of relying on whatever order the function happens to produce.

blocks.text: 5. One Hot Encoding: The Standard Fix for Non-Ordinal Categories

For categories with no real order, red, blue, green, or Mumbai, Delhi, Pune, the standard fix is one hot encoding. Instead of squeezing every category into one numeric column, you create a separate binary column for each category. Each new column holds a 1 if that row belongs to that category, and a 0 otherwise.

blocks.alt: One hot encoding creating a separate binary column for red, blue, and green from a single color column
blocks.caption: Each category gets its own independent 0 or 1 flag, so no fake numeric relationship gets introduced.

blocks.text: Because every one of these new columns is just an independent flag, there is no implied ordering and no implied distance between categories anymore. Green is not numerically close to or far from red, they are simply two separate yes or no columns. This is exactly what solves the false ordering problem from section 3.
6. The Dummy Variable Trap and drop_first

One hot encoding a column with N categories technically only needs N minus 1 columns, not N. If you have red, blue, and green, and you know a row is not red and not blue, it has to be green, there is no other option left. The third column is fully predictable from the other two, which makes it redundant.

blocks.alt: Three binary columns for red, blue, and green shown as redundant since the third is always predictable from the first two
blocks.caption: If is_red and is_blue are both 0, the row has to be green. Keeping all three columns wastes information you already have.

code.content:
df["is_red"] + df["is_blue"] + df["is_green"]
# always equals 1 for every single row, a perfectly predictable pattern

blocks.text: pandas' get_dummies() has a drop_first parameter built exactly for this. Set it to True and it drops the first category's column, keeping only N minus 1 columns.

code.content:
pd.get_dummies(df["color"], drop_first=True)

#    blue  green
# 0     0      0     (this row is red, implied by both columns being 0)
# 1     1      0
# 2     0      1

blocks.alt: drop_first removing the redundant red column and keeping only the blue and green columns
blocks.caption: Two columns instead of three, with zero loss of information.

blocks.text: This matters most for linear models. If you keep all N columns, those columns always sum to exactly 1 for every row, which is a perfect linear relationship between your own predictors. That is called perfect multicollinearity, and it breaks a core assumption behind linear and logistic regression. Depending on the solver, you can end up with unstable coefficients, or the model simply refusing to converge on a unique answer.

blocks.title: The dummy variable trap mostly bites linear models
blocks.content: Tree based models like random forests and gradient boosting are generally unaffected by keeping all N columns, since they do not rely on the same linear independence assumption. Even so, dropping one column with drop_first is a safe, sensible default habit no matter which model you end up using.

blocks.text: 7. The Real Cost of One Hot Encoding: Dimensionality Explosion

One hot encoding solves the false ordering problem completely, but it comes with a real practical cost: every unique category becomes an entirely new column. For a color column with three categories, that is barely noticeable. For a column with genuinely many unique values, it stops being harmless.

blocks.alt: A city column with 500 unique city names exploding into 500 new binary columns after one hot encoding
blocks.caption: High cardinality columns turn one hot encoding from a clean fix into a serious dimensionality problem.

blocks.text: Imagine a city column with 500 unique city names across your dataset. One hot encoding that single column creates 500 brand new columns, almost all of which will be 0 for any given row. Your dataframe balloons in width, most of the data becomes sparse, training slows down, and you run straight into what is often called the curse of dimensionality, where a model has to work far harder to find real patterns buried in a mostly empty, extremely wide feature space.
The width increase is easy to see directly. Picture a dataframe with 12 columns, one of which is that 500 category city column.

code.content:
df.shape
# (10000, 12)

pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["city"]).shape
# (10000, 511), five hundred new columns replacing just one

blocks.text: 7.1 Alternatives for High Cardinality Columns

When a column has too many unique values for one hot encoding to make sense, there are other techniques worth knowing exist, even though they are outside the scope of this lesson. Frequency encoding replaces each category with how often it appears in the dataset. Target encoding replaces each category with the average value of your target variable for that category, which can be powerful but also carries a real risk of leaking information from the target into your features if you are not careful.

blocks.alt: A high cardinality column being replaced with either a frequency count or an average target value per category
blocks.caption: Both approaches keep the column to a single number instead of hundreds of new columns, at the cost of some added complexity.

blocks.text: 8. Choosing Between Label Encoding and One Hot Encoding
By now the decision mostly comes down to one question: does the order of your categories mean something real? Everything else in this lesson flows from the answer.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Use this technique","Why"],"rows":[["Genuine natural order, like small, medium, large","Label encoding with an explicit mapping","The numeric order matches something real about the data"],["No natural order, like color, city, or product category","One hot encoding","Avoids inventing a false order and false distances between categories"],["Non-ordinal column with very many unique values","One hot encoding is risky, consider frequency or target encoding","Avoids a dimensionality explosion from hundreds of new columns"],["Feeding a linear or logistic regression model","One hot encoding with drop_first set to True","Prevents the dummy variable trap and perfect multicollinearity"]]}

blocks.title: A quick heuristic when you are not sure
blocks.content: Ask yourself: if I randomly swapped the order of two categories, would anything about their real world meaning change? If yes, the column is ordinal and label encoding with an explicit mapping is right. If swapping them changes nothing at all, the column is non-ordinal and one hot encoding is right.

blocks.text: 9. Worked Example: Size vs Color, Side by Side
The cleanest way to see the difference is to encode two columns from the exact same small dataset side by side, one genuinely ordinal, one genuinely not.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "size":  ["small", "large", "medium", "small", "large"],
    "color": ["red",   "blue",  "green",  "blue",  "red"],
})
print(df)

#     size  color
# 0  small    red
# 1  large   blue
# 2 medium  green
# 3  small   blue
# 4  large    red

blocks.text: 9.1 Encoding the Ordinal Size Column
size has a real order: small is genuinely smaller than medium, and medium is genuinely smaller than large. Label encoding with an explicit mapping is exactly right here.

code.content:
size_order = {"small": 0, "medium": 1, "large": 2}
df["size_encoded"] = df["size"].map(size_order)

print(df[["size", "size_encoded"]])

#     size  size_encoded
# 0  small             0
# 1  large             2
# 2 medium             1
# 3  small             0
# 4  large             2

blocks.alt: The size column small, medium, large label encoded to 0, 1, 2 using an explicit mapping
blocks.caption: One column in, one meaningful numeric column out. No new columns needed.

blocks.text: 9.2 Encoding the Non-Ordinal Color Column
color has no real order, red is not smaller or bigger than blue. One hot encoding, with drop_first to avoid the dummy variable trap, is the right call.

code.content:
color_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df["color"], prefix="color", drop_first=True)
df = pd.concat([df, color_dummies], axis=1)

print(df[["color", "color_green", "color_red"]])

#    color  color_green  color_red
# 0    red            0          1
# 1   blue            0          0
# 2  green            1          0
# 3   blue            0          0
# 4    red            0          1

blocks.alt: The color column red, blue, green one hot encoded into color_green and color_red binary columns with blue dropped
blocks.caption: Blue is implied whenever both new columns are 0. Nothing about red or green is treated as bigger or smaller.

blocks.text: 9.3 The Result, Side by Side

Look at what happened to each column. size went from three text values to a single numeric column where the numbers genuinely mean something. color went from three text values to two independent binary flags, specifically because forcing it into a single ordered number would have invented a relationship that was never there.

blocks.text: 10. Recap

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Label Encoding","One Hot Encoding"],"rows":[["What it produces","One numeric column with integer codes","One binary column per category"],["Best for","Genuinely ordinal categories with real order","Non-ordinal categories with no real order"],["Main risk","Implies a false order and false distance if used on non-ordinal data","Dimensionality explosion on high cardinality columns"],["Typical tools","pd.factorize(), sklearn LabelEncoder","pd.get_dummies()"]]}

items: Almost every ML algorithm needs pure numeric input, so text categories have to be converted before training.
Label encoding assigns each unique category an arbitrary integer, and it is fast, but that arbitrary order can be silently misread as meaningful by the model.
Use label encoding only for genuinely ordinal categories, and always supply an explicit mapping rather than trusting the default order.
One hot encoding creates one binary column per category and completely avoids the false ordering problem, making it the standard choice for non-ordinal data.
Use drop_first to avoid the dummy variable trap, especially before feeding one hot encoded columns into a linear or logistic regression model.
Watch out for high cardinality columns, since one hot encoding hundreds of unique categories creates hundreds of new columns and can hurt both memory and model performance.
